description: This team focuses on developing an autonomous, low-resource embedded flight core written in pure ISO C99 for closed-loop astronaut life support and biomedical telemetry regulation. The system is engineered to monitor oxygen, suit pressure, carbon dioxide levels, and thermal homeostasis automatically without ground-station dependency. This is a dedicated standalone project deployed directly to the Universal Event track.
summary:
AstroGuard ECLSS Core, developed by TAISSIANE THAIS DOS SANTOS, is a deterministic research and simulation prototype designed to explore environmental life-support monitoring and astronaut health telemetry during long-duration space missions.

The system integrates synthetic environmental and physiological measurements, including oxygen levels, pressure, temperature, heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, and fatigue indicators. A deterministic monitoring engine evaluates these simulated parameters and classifies conditions into normal, attention, and critical states.

The prototype includes telemetry records, automated tests, a browser-based monitoring dashboard, and mission visualization components. Its purpose is to demonstrate how integrated monitoring and explainable alerts could support situational awareness in future space exploration scenarios.

All telemetry data and decision thresholds are synthetic. The prototype is not a medical device or a flight-certified system.
details:
Project Overview

AstroGuard ECLSS Core is an autonomous, low-resource research and simulation software prototype developed by TAISSIANE THAIS DOS SANTOS. It explores integrated monitoring of environmental life-support conditions and astronaut physiological telemetry during long-duration space missions.

How It Works

The system simulates environmental parameters such as oxygen levels, pressure, temperature, and actuator states. It also simulates physiological parameters including heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO2), body temperature, respiratory rate, fatigue, and well-being.

A deterministic monitoring and decision engine processes the synthetic telemetry and identifies three operational states: NORMAL, ATTENTION, and CRITICAL.

Implemented Components

  • Environmental life-support simulation.
  • Human health monitoring layer.
  • Integrated synthetic telemetry stored in CSV format.
  • Deterministic state classification and verification scenarios.
  • Three-dimensional mission visualization.
  • Browser-based mission monitoring dashboard.
  • Automated unit and robustness tests.
  • Continuous integration through GitHub Actions.

Technologies

The prototype uses C for core monitoring logic, Python for visualization and supporting software, CSV for telemetry records, and web technologies for its browser-based dashboard. GitHub Actions supports automated verification.

Innovation and Expected Impact

AstroGuard explores the integration of environmental and physiological monitoring into a unified, explainable software architecture. Its deterministic approach makes simulated decisions reproducible and supports testing under controlled scenarios.

The project aims to contribute to research into monitoring architectures for future long-duration space exploration.

Scientific Scope

AstroGuard is a research and simulation prototype. All physiological telemetry, environmental scenarios, and decision thresholds are synthetic. It does not provide medical diagnoses, use actual astronaut health measurements, or claim NASA validation, medical certification, or flight qualification.

NASA Scientific Background

The project draws on NASA's "5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight" educational resource to contextualize the importance of astronaut health and environmental monitoring during long-duration space missions.

AstroGuard addresses this research theme through an integrated deterministic software prototype that simulates environmental and physiological telemetry, classifies monitoring conditions, and displays the resulting information through mission-oriented visualization interfaces.

NASA's resource is used as scientific background, not as a source of real astronaut telemetry or clinically validated decision thresholds.
